name: Jade Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a bank of six jacquard looms at a textile mill in the valley, we weave upholstery fabric for sofas and hotel chairs. A jacquard loom is the kind that can weave patterns, each thread lifted on its own, so you get flowers or stripes right in the cloth. I thread them up for new designs, mend broken threads, check the cloth for faults and keep the looms running. I love seeing a new pattern come off the beam for the first time. What wears me out is the noise, it's like standing inside a drum all day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside the mill?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Hugo, he fixes farm machinery, tractors mostly. We bought a little terraced house on Chapel Street last year, my parents helped with the deposit, and we've got about nine months of savings on top. I sing in the church choir on Thursdays and Sundays. We'd like children in the next few years, that's the big plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's one less thing to worry about, and get on with things. I might mention it in the choir group chat as a joke. I'm not one for big opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be pleased. I use an AI thing now and then, for the choir newsletter or to fix a recipe, and it's handy. If it stays a handy little helper for the choir newsletter, that's exactly where I want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep working at the mill, keep saving, get married next autumn like we planned, and think about children after that. Maybe ask about training as a loom technician, because they're paid better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the mill doing well, as far as you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's steady. We lost a big hotel order to a cheaper mill abroad last year, but we picked up two sofa makers. The owners are a family, third generation, and they look after people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the loom technician training involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a year of shadowing Gerald, our technician, and a short course. He's sixty and keeps saying he wants someone to hand over to. I'd want to do it before we have children.

S0.say: I'd say that's one less thing to worry about and get on with things. I might joke about it in the choir group chat, but I don't share big opinions online.
S0.think: Honestly, I'd be pleased, because I use AI now and then for small jobs and it's handy. That's exactly the size I want it to stay.
S0.do: Carries on at the mill, keeps saving and marries next autumn as planned. Considers training as a loom technician with the retiring technician before having children.
S0.quote: If it stays a handy little helper for the choir newsletter, that's exactly where I want it.
S0.fieldNote: Jade's life is carefully planned around marriage, a home and children, and she's comfortable with AI as an occasional helper. She respects the family-run mill and sees loyalty both ways. Her small ambition is to become a loom technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how business works, the mill has to keep up or it'll lose orders. But I'd also say a family firm should bring its workers along, not just swap them out. I'd say that kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit uneasy. The looms already run themselves mostly, it's the threading and the checking they'd try to automate. But I've seen the owners look after people before, so I'd trust them a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gerald to start teaching me the technician side sooner. I'd use the AI tools more to look up faults in the loom manuals. And I'd keep saving and keep the wedding plans as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly fine, but with one eye open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust the owners. What if they had to cut jobs anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'd do it, and I'd understand, it's their business. I'd rather the mill survived with fewer of us than closed with all of us. But I'd want them to be honest with us early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okafor, who does the cloth checking. She's been there twenty-five years and she spots faults no machine would. If they bring in a camera system, she'd be the first to go.

S1.say: I'd say it's how business works and the mill has to keep up, but a family firm should bring its workers along rather than swap them out.
S1.think: I'd be a bit uneasy, because the threading and the checking are the obvious things to automate. But I've seen the owners look after people before, so I'd trust them a bit.
S1.do: Asks the technician to start training her sooner and uses AI tools more to look up loom faults. Keeps saving and keeps her wedding plans unchanged.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly fine but with one eye open.
S1.quote: I'd rather the mill survived with fewer of us than closed with all of us.
S1.fieldNote: Jade accepts the business logic of cuts while asking for honesty and loyalty. She'd rather the mill survive smaller than close. She speeds up her technician training rather than looking elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and it shows that people in charge, in companies and in government, didn't think it through. I'd say families and communities will have to hold things together, like they always have. I'd say it at church, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the mill would go robotic or close within a year or so. I'd be worried, but I've got Hugo, the house and the savings. I'd be scared more for the future, for the kids we haven't had yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder and cut anything extra. I think, oddly, I'd want to bring the wedding forward and have children sooner, while we both still have wages. And I'd lean on my parents and the church community, because that's what they're there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Worried, but not lost. I'd still feel I had people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have children sooner, not later? Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather have a baby while we're both earning than wait for a world that might be worse. If the jobs are going anyway, I'd rather spend my last years at the mill saving for a cot. Hugo might take some convincing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to learn anything new in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I wouldn't know what. If it can do almost any job, I'd rather focus on the family and the house. I'd trust that we'd work something out together.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and shows that companies and government didn't think it through. Families and communities will have to hold things together, like always.
S2.think: I think the mill would go robotic or close within a year or so. I've got Hugo, the house and the savings, so I'd be scared mostly for the kids we haven't had yet.
S2.do: Saves harder and cuts extras, and wants to bring the wedding and children forward while both still earn. Leans on her parents and church community.
S2.feel: Anxious but not lost, with people around her.
S2.quote: If the jobs are going anyway, I'd rather spend my last years at the mill saving for a cot.
S2.fieldNote: Jade's surprising response to fast AGI is to have children sooner, not later. Her sense of security comes from family, faith and the house more than from her job. She doesn't try to retrain because she can't see what for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so families and communities should start planning together. I'd say the government should help with apprenticeships for people changing trade. Practical help, not just money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years would let me do something. I'd think about a job where people still want a person, like a healthcare assistant at the maternity ward. I know robots might do that too one day, but I think people will want a real hand to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the loom technician training first, because it pays better for now. Then around year two I'd start a part-time healthcare assistant course. We'd get married next autumn as planned and think about children around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A lot calmer than the two-year one, because I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maternity, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister had her first baby last year, and the healthcare assistant who stayed with her all night was the one she talked about afterwards, not the doctors. I'd like to be that person for someone, even if a robot can do the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can do things in order. Technician, then course, then children. With two years I'd have to grab at everything at once.

S3.say: I'd say families and communities should start planning together now, and the government should help with apprenticeships for people changing trade.
S3.think: Five years would let me move towards work where people still want a person, like being a healthcare assistant on a maternity ward. I think people will want a real hand to hold.
S3.do: Finishes loom technician training, then starts a part-time healthcare assistant course around year two. Marries next autumn as planned and plans children around year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but much calmer than in the two-year picture because she has a plan.
S3.quote: I'd like to be that person for someone, even if a robot can do the paperwork.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Jade puts things in order: technician, course, children. Her interest in maternity care comes from a family story, not a career chart. She knows robots might reach care work but believes people will want a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people plan, and that's what families have always done. I'd say young people should learn trades and that work matters. And companies should help the towns they've done well in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with two little ones. There'd be time to move into healthcare before the mill changed too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the technician training, get married, and have our first child in the next couple of years. Around year four or five I'd start the healthcare course and move across. Hugo and I would keep saving every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a quiet way. More hopeful than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave the mill after ten years there. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, honestly. I'll miss the moment a new pattern comes off the loom, even if a robot can watch it just as well. But I'd rather leave on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change how you use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit more, once everyone else was using it. If it helps me pass a course or keep track of my shifts, I'd use it. I'm not against it, I just don't need to be first.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if people plan, as families always have. Young people should learn trades, and companies should help the towns they've done well in.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable. I'd be thirty-seven, probably with two little ones, and I'd have time to move into healthcare before the mill changed too much.
S4.do: Takes the technician training, marries and has a first child within a couple of years. Starts a healthcare course around year four or five and moves across, while saving every month.
S4.quote: I'll miss the moment a new pattern comes off the loom, even if a robot can watch it just as well.
S4.fieldNote: Jade's ten-year plan is calm and family-first, with a career change slotted in around children. She'd miss the craft of the loom but wants to leave on her own terms. She'd pick up AI more once others had.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would come before we've even had children. I always pictured my kids visiting me at the mill, like I visited my dad at the bus depot. What would help is apprenticeships and courses that pay a wage, and support for young families, so having children doesn't feel like a gamble.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what role church and family play. People forget those. When things go wrong, that's who turns up.

headlineQuote: I always pictured my kids visiting me at the mill, like I visited my dad at the bus depot.
portrait: Jade is a 27-year-old jacquard loom operator at a family-owned textile mill, engaged to a farm machinery mechanic and living in a terraced house bought with her parents' help. She sings in the church choir, uses AI now and then, and plans her life around marriage and children. She's calm in the plateau and uneasy in steady disruption, and in fast AGI she becomes anxious but surprisingly decides to have children sooner. With more time she plans a careful path from loom technician to maternity healthcare assistant.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because it would arrive before she and Hugo have even had children.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and courses that pay a wage, plus support for young families so having children doesn't feel like a gamble.
